topic.official-figures-consistency.text: Whether each official figure follows from the data the same office publishes, and what explains it when it doesn’t.
topic.official-figures-consistency.quest: Do the official figures add up?
m5.lead: Official statistics are built from other published numbers: a yearly inflation rate from a price index, a price index from the prices of hundreds of things. So anyone should be able to rebuild them from what is published. We do, figure by figure, and show where they fit and where they don’t.
m5.stat.agree: agree; every other one is listed, with its cause or what we know so far
m5.filter.label: Show checks
m5.key.explained: some figures don’t fit, and we know why
m5.key.agree: every figure fits, or differs only by rounding
m5.note.rounding: The other {n} differ only by rounding: the published figures are rounded, so the last digit can differ.
m5.check.gr-cpi-rates-own-index.title: The CPI’s yearly rates against its own index
m5.check.gr-cpi-rates-own-index.question: Does the published inflation rate follow from the published price index?
m5.check.gr-cpi-rates-own-index.text: ELSTAT’s table 05 publishes the consumer price index and its change on the same month a year before. Each rate should equal the index over the index a year earlier. We check every month at full precision.
m5.check.gr-cpi-rates-rebuilt.title: The CPI’s yearly rates against the index in table 07
m5.check.gr-cpi-rates-rebuilt.question: Do ELSTAT’s two tables of the price index give the same inflation rate?
m5.check.gr-cpi-rates-rebuilt.text: Table 07 publishes the overall index again, next to the index of every item. We compute the yearly rate from it, each year from its own file, and compare it with table 05’s rate at full precision.
m5.check.gr-cpi-rebuilt-items.title: The CPI rebuilt from its items and weights
m5.check.gr-cpi-rebuilt-items.question: Does the price index add up from the prices of the things in it?
m5.check.gr-cpi-rebuilt-items.text: We rebuild the overall index from the index and weight of every item ELSTAT publishes, and compare the yearly rates once rounded to one decimal, as published. The items and weights are themselves published rounded, so a rebuilt rate can be 0.1 off: that is rounding.
m5.check.gr-hicp-rebuilt-items.title: The harmonised index (HICP) rebuilt
m5.check.gr-hicp-rebuilt-items.question: Does Europe’s harmonised price index for Greece add up from its parts?
m5.check.gr-hicp-rebuilt-items.text: The same for the harmonised index Eurostat publishes for Greece: rebuilt from the index and weight of every item, compared once rounded to one decimal.
m5.check.gr-hbs-household-types.title: Household types in the spending survey
m5.check.gr-hbs-household-types.question: Does the survey sort households the way Eurostat’s rule says?
m5.check.gr-hbs-household-types.source: ELSTAT’s own type against Eurostat’s written rule
m5.check.gr-hbs-household-types.text: The survey’s public file holds ELSTAT’s own household type. We build the six types from each person’s relationship and activity by Eurostat’s written rule and compare each type’s share of households, year by year. Shares within one percentage point count as agreeing.
m5.check.gr-hbs-spending.title: Spending in the survey’s published table
m5.check.gr-hbs-spending.question: Does the survey’s published spending table match the survey’s own data?
m5.check.gr-hbs-spending.source: ELSTAT’s table 1.03 against the same survey’s public file
m5.check.gr-hbs-spending.text: ELSTAT publishes the household budget survey’s average monthly spending on each item (table 1.03), and the survey’s file of households too. We add up the file with its own weights and compare every item, year by year, and each income or size band where the bands can be rebuilt (2010–2013). Figures within a cent count as agreeing. Items the file leaves out or cuts (tolls, life insurance and a few more) aren’t compared.

m5.question.gr-renters.title: What share of households rent their home?
m5.question.gr-renters.text: The census counts every household. The income survey (EU-SILC) fits its weights to the census’s number of renters, from 2023 to the 2021 census, so it agrees with the census by design: the census is the one independent count. The household spending survey has no such adjustment and finds fewer renters, and the gap has grown since 2011. Households and persons are counted separately, since the sources don’t all count both.
m5.question.gr-renters.teaser: The census and the income survey agree. The spending survey finds about a third fewer renters.
m5.question.gr-rent-paid.title: How much rent do households pay?
m5.question.gr-rent-paid.text: The two surveys, the national accounts and the tax returns give very different totals. Part of the gap is definition: the tax figure counts all property, not only homes. The national accounts’ rent rises 45% in 2021 because ELSTAT rebuilt its housing stock on the 2021 census: most of the rise is rent moved from owners’ imputed rent to tenants’ actual rent, so the years before 2021 are not on the same footing as those after.
m5.question.gr-rent-paid.teaser: Four sources give a yearly total, and not all of them count the same rent. How far apart are they?
m5.question.gr-household-income.title: How much income do households have?
m5.question.gr-household-income.text: The national accounts estimate all income, declared or not; the tax returns count only what is declared. The surveys’ own income limits are compared in their own question.
m5.question.gr-household-income.teaser: Tax returns and the national accounts both count households’ income, but not the same income.
m5.question.gr-unemployment.title: How many people are unemployed?
m5.question.gr-unemployment.text: The labour force survey counts people with no work who are looking and available; the employment service’s register counts everyone registered as unemployed by its own rules. In the crisis years the survey counted more (1.34 million in 2013, against the register’s 1.04 million); since 2018 the register has counted more, and in 2024 almost twice as many (896,000 against 480,000).
m5.question.gr-unemployment.teaser: The employment service’s register and the labour force survey count the unemployed by different rules.

m5.question.gr-rent-weight.title: How much of household spending goes on rent?
m5.question.gr-rent-weight.text: Each price index weighs rent by its share of household spending. The CPI and the HICP take that share from the household budget survey, which counts about a third fewer renters than the 2021 census, so rent may weigh too little in them; the national accounts count rented homes from the census.
m5.question.gr-rent-weight.teaser: How much of households’ spending goes on rent? The price indices, the national accounts and the spending survey each answer.
m5.question.gr-rent-change.title: How fast do rents rise?
m5.question.gr-rent-change.text: Each line is set to 100 in 2015. From 2015 to 2021 the CPI’s rent index fell by about 8% and then hardly moved, while the average rent renters report paying rose: by about 19% in the household budget survey and 9% in EU-SILC. By 2024 the CPI’s index was 3% above 2015, the two surveys 34% and 23%. An average rent is not a price index: it also moves with who rents what. Why the CPI’s rent index stayed flat is not known. No other rent series can serve as a check: the rent figures the Bank of Greece and the OECD publish are the CPI’s own rent index.
m5.question.gr-rent-change.teaser: Since 2015 the CPI’s rent index has risen 3%. The rent households say they pay has risen 23% to 34%.

m5.question.gr-income-limits.title: Where does each income fifth end?
m5.question.gr-income-limits.text: Our limits from the household spending survey, next to Eurostat’s from the income survey, for the same year’s incomes. The two surveys measure income differently, so a gap of a few percent is expected. In 2011–2014 the spending survey’s own incomes stand higher against the national accounts than in other years (0.69–0.83 of household disposable income, against about 0.6), so the far larger gap in 2012–2014 comes from that survey, not from the income survey or our method. Why those years stand higher is not known. In 2010 our limits fall far below Eurostat’s instead: the survey’s wage incomes that year are a fraction of the years either side (renting households’ median money income €6,680 a year, against €17,800 in 2009 and €14,000 in 2011), in ELSTAT’s own published income table too; why is not known either.
m5.question.gr-income-limits.teaser: Where does the poorest fifth’s income end? Our spending-survey limit and Eurostat’s income-survey limit, year by year.

option.heading: Method options
reason.rule_f_start: Rule F takes the survey of three years before. The oldest survey with public microdata is 2008, so Rule F's weights start in 2011.
reason.rule_u_end: Rule U takes the same year's survey. The newest survey with public microdata is {survey}, so Rule U stops at {month}.
reason.same_before_2026: The two tutoring options differ only from 2026, when ELSTAT's CPI stops weighting tutoring; before that they are the same series.
reason.hospital: The {first}–{last} household surveys' public files leave out hospital services. Putting them back changes the groups' annual-average rates by at most 0.11 points and the gap by at most 0.07 points.
reason.lockdown: Weights from the 2020 survey, a lockdown year with unusual spending.
reason.first_estimate: A first estimate: the weights will be revised once, when the survey of the year before is out.
reason.fixed_lag: Our choice: before our archive existed, survey release dates can't be used, so Rule F is a fixed lag of three years, today's lag.
reason.less_certain: CPI prices for 2009–2010 come from ELSTAT's original tables, an older version of the prices.
reason.coarser_detail: Before 2015, Eurostat's Greek HICP has item indices only for broader categories, so the items within one share its price movement.
reason.same_year_weights: Same-year weights: not a Laspeyres-type index (its weights aren't from before the prices). Shown to compare with studies made after the fact.
reason.starts_later: Not available before {month}: this option's source starts later.
reason.ends_earlier: Not yet published for {month}: this option's source releases later than ELSTAT's CPI.
reason.hicp_later: Eurostat publishes the HICP's item indices about a week after ELSTAT's CPI, so these combinations update later in the month.
reason.timing.N: Newest survey up to the year before; revised once when that survey's microdata arrive.

income.lead: What a household takes home after tax decides its group. A bigger household needs more money for the same standard of living, so the limits depend on who lives with you.

income.source.ours_note: Household budget survey {survey}, which describes {income} incomes. Each limit is the midpoint between the two surveyed households either side of it, rounded to the euro: never one household's income alone (if the two report the same income, both share it). Because the survey asks only a sample of households, each limit has a standard error: {se_from} to {se_to} for one adult.
income.source.compare: For {income} incomes, Eurostat puts the poorest 20%'s limit for one adult at {eurostat}, we put it at {ours}: {diff}. Why they differ is explained below.
income.unit.pps_none: Not available for our figures yet: Eurostat hasn't published its purchasing power conversion for {income} incomes.
income.unit.note.gr: an artificial currency that buys the same goods and services in every country, so incomes can be compared across countries. In Greece a euro buys more than one PPS's worth: Eurostat counts an income of {eur} as {pps}.
income.why: Why our figures and Eurostat's differ
income.why1: Our figures come from the household budget survey, the same survey our groups are built from. Eurostat's come from a different survey (EU-SILC), the official source for incomes.
income.why2: Eurostat takes property tax, the self-employed's insurance contributions and money paid regularly to other households off income. The household budget survey doesn't take off the first two, and takes off the third only from 2024, if at all: ELSTAT hasn't said. That alone would put our limits a few percent above Eurostat's. The gap we measure is often larger, as the line above shows: the two surveys ask different households, in different ways, and people report their income differently to each. We show both rather than adjust one to the other.
